blocks.text: A 44-year-old delivery driver has had three minor collisions in a month, each time clipping a vehicle on his left or right as he passed. Looking straight ahead he sees well, but his side vision is gone in both eyes. Where the two optic nerves meet, a small structure has been squeezing the fibres that carry the outer visual field.

blocks.markdown:
**The retina.** Light passes through the inner retinal layers to reach the **photoreceptors**: **rods** (dim light, no colour, high sensitivity) and **cones** (bright light, colour, high acuity, concentrated in the **macula** and **fovea**). Photoreceptors synapse on **bipolar cells**, which synapse on **retinal ganglion cells**. The ganglion cell axons form the **optic nerve (cranial nerve II)**. Horizontal and amacrine cells modulate the signal laterally. The optic disc, where axons leave, has no photoreceptors and is the physiological blind spot.

**Visual fields and retinal halves.** The lens inverts the image, so the **temporal visual field** falls on the **nasal retina** and the **nasal visual field** falls on the **temporal retina**. The left visual field of both eyes is therefore processed by the right hemisphere.

**The pathway.** Retinal ganglion cell axons run in the **optic nerve**, to the **optic chiasm**, where fibres from the **nasal retina** (carrying the temporal field) **cross**, while fibres from the temporal retina stay uncrossed. Beyond the chiasm the fibres form the **optic tract**, which carries the *contralateral* visual field from both eyes. Most synapse in the **lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN)** of the thalamus. From there the **optic radiation** fibres run to the **primary visual cortex (V1)** in the occipital lobe along the **calcarine sulcus**.

In the optic radiation, fibres carrying the **superior** visual field loop through the temporal lobe (**Meyer loop**), whereas fibres carrying the **inferior** visual field pass through the parietal lobe. Some optic tract fibres go instead to the **pretectal area** (pupillary reflex) and **superior colliculus** (eye movements).

blocks.title: Where the fibres cross
blocks.text: Only nasal retinal fibres cross at the optic chiasm. Each optic tract, LGN, radiation and visual cortex therefore represents the contralateral half of the visual field for both eyes.

rows: Complete loss of vision in that eye (monocular)
blocks.caption: A homonymous defect affects the same side of the visual field in both eyes.

blocks.title: Right optic tract lesion
blocks.prompt: A right optic tract is cut. Predict the field defect and explain it.

steps.text: The right optic tract carries fibres from the right temporal retina (uncrossed, seeing the left nasal field) and from the left nasal retina (crossed, seeing the left temporal field).
Therefore the right tract represents the whole left visual field of both eyes.
Cutting it removes the left visual field in both eyes, which is a left homonymous hemianopia.

blocks.answer: A left homonymous hemianopia: the left half of the visual field is lost in both eyes.

blocks.markdown: **The chiasm.** The optic chiasm lies just above the pituitary gland, at the base of the brain, with the hypothalamus above. A mass pressing on the chiasm from below, such as a pituitary adenoma, compresses the crossing nasal fibres first, producing **bitemporal hemianopia**, often beginning in the upper temporal quadrants. Pressure from above, as with a craniopharyngioma, may affect lower fields first. Uncrossed fibres at the lateral chiasm are spared, so a lesion at the chiasm does not cause loss of the nasal fields.

blocks.title: Pupillary light reflex
blocks.text: Light on one retina causes constriction of both pupils: the direct reflex in the stimulated eye and the consensual reflex in the opposite eye. The afferent limb is the optic nerve (CN II); the efferent limb is the parasympathetic fibres of the oculomotor nerve (CN III).

items: Retinal ganglion cell axons travel in the optic nerve and tract and, before the LGN, branch to the pretectal area of the midbrain.
Each pretectal nucleus sends signals to both Edinger-Westphal nuclei, so each eye's input reaches both sides.
Preganglionic parasympathetic fibres leave the Edinger-Westphal nucleus with the oculomotor nerve and synapse in the ciliary ganglion.
Postganglionic fibres travel in the short ciliary nerves to the sphincter pupillae, which constricts the pupil (miosis).

blocks.title: Light reflex with an afferent defect
blocks.prompt: A patient has complete blindness from a right optic nerve lesion, but normal oculomotor nerves. Predict the pupil responses to light in each eye.

steps.text: Light in the right eye: the afferent signal cannot leave the right retina, so neither pupil constricts.
Light in the left eye: the left optic nerve is intact, so signals reach the pretectal area and both Edinger-Westphal nuclei.
Both oculomotor nerves are intact, so the left pupil constricts (direct) and the right pupil constricts (consensual).

blocks.answer: Light in the right eye produces no constriction in either pupil; light in the left eye constricts both. The pattern shows an afferent (optic nerve) problem rather than an efferent one.

blocks.title: Afferent versus efferent
blocks.text: If both pupils respond when you shine light in one eye but not the other, the problem is afferent in the unresponsive eye. If one pupil fails to constrict whichever eye is lit, the efferent limb (CN III) on that side is affected.

points: Retinal ganglion cell axons form the optic nerve; nasal retinal fibres cross at the optic chiasm.
Optic tract, LGN, optic radiation and V1 represent the contralateral visual field of both eyes.
Lesion site predicts the defect: monocular loss for the nerve, bitemporal hemianopia for the chiasm, homonymous defects beyond the chiasm.
The pupillary light reflex runs retina, optic nerve, pretectal area, both Edinger-Westphal nuclei, CN III, ciliary ganglion, sphincter pupillae.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes the visual pathway from the retina to the cortex?

options.text: Optic nerve, optic chiasm, optic tract, lateral geniculate nucleus, optic radiation, primary visual cortex
Optic nerve, lateral geniculate nucleus, optic chiasm, optic tract, optic radiation, primary visual cortex
Optic tract, optic chiasm, optic nerve, optic radiation, lateral geniculate nucleus, primary visual cortex
Optic nerve, optic chiasm, optic radiation, lateral geniculate nucleus, optic tract, primary visual cortex

questions.correctOptionText: Optic nerve, optic chiasm, optic tract, lateral geniculate nucleus, optic radiation, primary visual cortex

distractorRationale.b: The LGN lies after the chiasm and tract, not before.
distractorRationale.c: The nerve precedes the chiasm and tract.
distractorRationale.d: The optic radiation arises from the LGN; it does not precede it.

questions.explanation: Ganglion cell axons form the optic nerve, cross partly at the chiasm, continue as the optic tract to the LGN, and the optic radiation carries the signal onward to V1.

questions.stem: Which fibres decussate at the optic chiasm?

options.text: Fibres from the temporal retina of each eye
Fibres from the nasal retina of each eye

questions.correctOptionText: Fibres from the nasal retina of each eye

distractorRationale.a: Temporal retinal fibres stay on the same side.
distractorRationale.b: Not all fibres cross; temporal retinal fibres remain ipsilateral.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: nasal retinal fibres, which see the temporal field, cross.
distractorRationale.d: Macular fibres follow the same rule as the rest of the retina.

questions.explanation: Fibres from the nasal retina, which represent the temporal visual field, cross at the chiasm. Temporal retinal fibres do not cross, so each tract carries the contralateral hemifield.

questions.stem: The axons of which retinal cell type form the optic nerve?

distractorRationale.b: Bipolar cells synapse on ganglion cells but do not leave the retina.
distractorRationale.c: Amacrine cells are local modulating interneurones.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: ganglion cell axons exit at the optic disc.

questions.explanation: The retinal circuit runs photoreceptor to bipolar cell to ganglion cell. Only ganglion cell axons leave the eye, gathering at the optic disc to form the optic nerve.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman has headaches and amenorrhoea. Visual field testing shows progressive loss of the outer half of the visual field in both eyes. Which lesion site best explains this?

options.text: Optic chiasm, compressing the crossing nasal retinal fibres
Primary visual cortex on one side

questions.correctOptionText: Optic chiasm, compressing the crossing nasal retinal fibres

distractorRationale.a: Correct: loss of both temporal fields (bitemporal hemianopia) is typical of chiasmal compression, for example by a pituitary mass.
distractorRationale.b: A tract lesion causes a homonymous defect, on the same side in both eyes.
distractorRationale.c: An optic nerve lesion causes monocular loss.
distractorRationale.d: A cortical lesion causes a homonymous defect.

questions.explanation: Loss of the outer (temporal) half of each visual field is bitemporal hemianopia, which results from interruption of the crossing fibres of the nasal retinae at the chiasm. The headache and amenorrhoea suggest a pituitary mass pressing on the chiasm.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man has a left temporal lobe tumour that interrupts the loop of optic radiation fibres through the temporal lobe. What visual field defect is expected?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the left temporal Meyer loop carries the right superior visual field.
distractorRationale.b: The left optic radiation represents the right visual field, not the left.
distractorRationale.c: Inferior field fibres pass through the parietal lobe.

questions.explanation: The left optic radiation carries the right visual field. Superior-field fibres loop through the temporal lobe, so interrupting them gives a right superior quadrantanopia.

questions.stem: True or false: a lesion confined to the midline of the optic chiasm causes loss of the nasal half of the visual field in both eyes.
questions.explanation: A midline chiasmal lesion damages the crossing nasal retinal fibres, which carry the temporal visual fields, so the defect is bitemporal, not binasal. Nasal fields depend on uncrossed temporal retinal fibres that run at the sides of the chiasm.

questions.stem: In which structure are the preganglionic parasympathetic neurones for the pupillary light reflex located?

distractorRationale.a: The superior cervical ganglion supplies sympathetic fibres to the dilator pupillae.
distractorRationale.b: The LGN is the relay for vision, not the pupillary reflex.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: preganglionic fibres arise in the Edinger-Westphal nucleus and travel with CN III.
distractorRationale.d: The trochlear nucleus supplies superior oblique.

questions.explanation: The Edinger-Westphal nucleus gives rise to the parasympathetic fibres that travel with the oculomotor nerve to the ciliary ganglion. Its postganglionic fibres supply the sphincter pupillae.

questions.stem: A patient has a complete left oculomotor nerve palsy with a normal right eye and normal optic nerves. A torch is shone into the right eye. What happens to the pupils?

options.text: The left pupil constricts and the right does not
The right pupil constricts and the left does not

questions.correctOptionText: The right pupil constricts and the left does not

distractorRationale.a: The left sphincter pupillae has lost its CN III supply and cannot constrict.
distractorRationale.b: The right eye's afferent and efferent pathways are intact.
distractorRationale.c: This reverses the pattern; the left efferent pathway is damaged.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: right direct reflex works, but the left consensual response fails because its efferent limb is CN III.

questions.explanation: The afferent limb from the right eye is normal, and signals reach both Edinger-Westphal nuclei. The right efferent limb works, so the right pupil constricts; the left efferent limb (CN III) is damaged, so the left pupil cannot respond.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man has a stroke that destroys the left primary visual cortex (calcarine cortex) but spares the midbrain. Describe the visual field defect and predict whether his pupillary light reflexes are preserved, giving the anatomical reason.
markingGuide: Right homonymous hemianopia (the left V1 represents the right visual field of both eyes)
Possible macular sparing may be mentioned but is not required
Retinal fibres for the reflex leave the optic tract before the LGN and synapse in the pretectal area of the midbrain
Pretectal signals go to both Edinger-Westphal nuclei, so the reflex arc does not involve the cortex
questions.explanation: The left V1 receives the right visual field from both eyes, so its destruction causes a right homonymous hemianopia. The pupillary reflex is subcortical, relying on the pretectal area and Edinger-Westphal nuclei, so it remains intact despite cortical blindness in that hemifield.

questions.stem: Trace the path of light from an object in the patient's left visual field to the primary visual cortex. Name the retinal half involved in each eye, where fibres cross or stay uncrossed, and the cortical destination.
markingGuide: The left visual field falls on the right temporal retina of the right eye and the left nasal retina of the left eye
Ganglion cell axons travel in the optic nerves
Left nasal fibres cross at the optic chiasm; right temporal fibres do not
Both streams unite in the right optic tract
Synapse in the right lateral geniculate nucleus
Optic radiation to the right primary visual cortex along the calcarine sulcus of the occipital lobe
questions.explanation: The lens inverts the image, so the left visual field lands on the right temporal and left nasal retinae. Because the nasal fibres decussate at the chiasm, the right optic tract carries the whole left field to the right LGN and then to right V1.
